Decoding LLM Alignment: A Concise Guide for GRPO and its variants

Community Article Published
October 4, 2026 Upvote 5 Sneha Rudra Sneha7
Training & aligning Large Language & Vision Models with reinforcement learning has shifted dramatically. We have moved away from complex actor-critic setups towards group normalized and sequence-level optimization algorithms.
Whether you are designing an LLM post-training pipeline or scaling a reasoning model or preparing for an AI interview, keeping track of these advancements can be overwhelming. This concise guide breaks down the core reinforecement learning algorithms powering todays open & proprietary models. We will cover 6 methods - PPO, RLOO, GRPO, Pref-GRPO, GSPO & GDPO.

1. The Complete Comparison Table

During RL (Reinforcement Learning) training for LLMs, algorithms update the weights of the policy model - aka the LLM being aligned -- to favor outputs with higher advantage - which is a measure of how much better or worse a sampled completion is; compared to a baseline.

Method
What problem is it solving?
How does it work?
When to use it?
Big Picture in the RL revolution

PPO

Proximal Policy Optimization
Reliable (i.e stable training) policy optimization for RLHF
- Critic model outputs a value estimate for each token. Think of the value estimate as - is how good is the rest of completion likely to be if we continue from that token. - Clipped policy gradients.
- When you need token level precision -Have the memory/ compute to afford a critic network -Have human labelled preference pairs
The Classic Standard that RLHF uses.

RLOO

REINFORCE Leave-One-Out
Massive hardware overhead of keeping an extra critic in memory
- Drops the critic - Uses the average rewards of other completions in a group of rollout to get baseline
When you want to scale alignment
The Efficiency Pivot. Shifted the industry away from heavy critic setups

GRPO

Group Relative Policy Optimization
High compute costs associated with training a model to reason through math & code
-Samples multiple completions for a given prompt - Computes advantage for each by subtracting the group's mean reward from the completion's reward
When training math/ coding models with automated verifiers
Unlocked the reasoning era - core engine behind reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1

Pref-GRPO

Preference GRPO
- Scaler rewards get games easily when rewards scores withn a group are near identical
Instead of raw scores, uses pair wise winrate within a group as reward signal
- When you want to align a model using a preference pair data without a separate critic/ verifier model - Alignment involves multiple subjective criteria
Incorporated human preference signals in GRPO

GSPO

Group Sequence Policy Optimization
Noisy updates ie. high variance in gradients & training crashes while training MoEs for reasoning
Moves all the optimization math (ratios, clipping) to full sequence ie completion level instead of token level
For large scale model training eg MoEs
Enabled oong horizon reasoning for large sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) models

GDPO

Group Reward Decoupled Policy Optimization
Reward signal collapses when adding competing goals, washing out granular tradeoffs
Normalize each reward goal independently before adding
When you are balancing competing criteria eg accuracy, safety, brevity
Enabled multi-objective alignment under conflicting real world constraints

2. Visual Walkthrough - How the rollouts are treated differently?

To understand how these RL methods work under the hood, lets take a look at how they process a group of K completions generated by the policy model for a given single prompt.

To conclude, as RL for language models moves beyond a single reward and a single training recipe, understanding how each method constructs its learning signal is essential for choosing the right tool for the behavior you want to optimize.
